title: Ulyana and the Interior
premise: Ivo Villalobos, a court translator who has spent thirty years erasing herself into other people's words, hears a song on a late-night radio program that was written by her mother and never recorded—a song that exists only in the memory of the village she fled as a child. Tracing it to a dying folklorist who taped it decades ago, Ivo discovers the recording also contains her father's voice confessing to a crime the village blamed on an innocent man, a man now old and imprisoned. To bring justice without destroying what remains of her family's name, Ivo must translate the confession from a language she is losing word by word, racing against both the archive's decay and the prisoner's failing health. In the end she chooses truth over invisibility: she publishes the translation under her own name, loses the last of her childhood language, and gains—for the first time—a self that is entirely hers.
about_author: Lior Thornbury is the pen name of a former interpreter who worked in immigration courts for eleven years before leaving to write. They live near a border town where three languages are spoken in the same kitchen, and none of them is their first.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Ivo, a fifty-three-year-old court translator who has made a discipline of disappearing—flawless work, no opinions, no attachments. A routine day rendering testimony shows her gift and her armor. When a colleague invites her to dinner, she deploys the smile. Emotional beat: the quiet ache of a life built entirely out of other people's sentences.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV deepens through her nightly ritual of testing her dwindling childhood language, Kavreni, against a pocket dictionary, noting which words have gone dark. Her therapist calls it attrition; Ivo calls it shedding. She translates a deportation hearing with chilling precision. Beat: grief disguised as professionalism; the reader learns language loss is her oldest wound.

chapters.title: A Song That Was Never Recorded
chapters.summary: Driving home at 2 a.m., Ivo hears a folk song on a university radio hour—and recognizes it as one her mother composed and sang only once, in a kitchen, in 1979. It cannot exist. She pulls over, shaking. The host credits 'field recordings, V. Aranov collection.' Beat: vertigo—the past reaching through the radio to claim her.

chapters.title: The Archivist's Answering Machine
chapters.summary: Ivo tracks the collection to retired folklorist Vera Aranov, now in a care facility. Phone calls go unanswered; Ivo leaves messages she immediately regrets. Flashback seeds: the village of Zelenmoor, the night the family left. Beat: reluctance warring with compulsion—Ivo drafts three retreats and cancels all of them.

chapters.title: Room 114
chapters.summary: Ivo visits Vera, who is sharp-tongued and half-blind but remembers everything she ever taped. Vera plays the song; then, unprompted, says there is more on that reel—'a voice after the singing.' Ivo asks whose. Vera: 'You'll know it when you hear it.' Beat: dread blooming; the door opens and Ivo steps through anyway.

chapters.title: Her Father's Voice
chapters.summary: In the archive listening room, Ivo hears her father, aged thirty, confessing in Kavreni to a fire that killed the miller—an arson the village pinned on Tomas Brandt, who went to prison. The recording cuts off mid-sentence. Ivo recognizes every word except the crucial final clause, which her lost vocabulary can no longer parse. Beat: devastation; the untranslatable sentence named.

chapters.title: What the Village Knew
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, young Ivo's POV, 1979–80: the fire, the arrest of gentle Tomas Brandt, her parents' hushed arguments, the family's flight. Child-Ivo adored her father and feared his silences. Beat: dramatic irony fulfilled—the reader now understands what the child only sensed.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Guilt
chapters.summary: Present day: Ivo attempts to reconstruct the missing clause from memory and fails; Kavreni's subjunctive, the key to whether her father confessed or confessed-for-someone, has slipped away. She consults a linguistics professor, Dr. Okafor, who confirms fewer than two hundred speakers remain. Beat: rising stakes—the truth hinges on grammar she no longer owns.

chapters.title: Tomas Brandt Is Still Alive
chapters.summary: Okafor locates a speaker registry; Ivo finds Tomas Brandt listed—released after twenty-two years, now eighty-one, living in a coastal nursing home, dying of heart failure. He was convicted partly on testimony her father never gave but never refuted. Beat: moral urgency crystallizes; time limit established.

chapters.title: The Reel Degrades
chapters.summary: Vera's tape begins to shed its oxide layer; a preservation lab gives it months, maybe weeks. Ivo pays for emergency digitization, but the damaged section is precisely the confession's end. Meanwhile her sister Marisol calls from abroad, warning her not to dig up the family. Beat: twin clocks ticking—tape and man.

chapters.title: Marisol
chapters.summary: Sister-POV interlude: Marisol, who stayed loyal to the family myth, reveals she has always known something was wrong with the fire story and chose silence to protect their mother's memory. She begs Ivo to let the dead stay buried. Beat: love against duty, first articulation; the sisters' fracture line drawn.

chapters.title: Learning My Mother Tongue Like a Stranger
chapters.summary: Ivo throws herself into relearning Kavreni with Okafor and an elderly speaker, Mrs. Ferreol, via video calls. Words return unevenly, attached to smells and fears rather than definitions. She re-transcribes the confession nightly, each pass yielding new nuance. Beat: tentative hope; the theme of recovery-through-loss inverted.

chapters.title: The Subjunctive
chapters.summary: Breakthrough: Mrs. Ferreol hears the damaged passage and identifies a construction meaning 'if it must be said'—conditional, protective, possibly implicating someone else. But the subject noun is destroyed. Ivo realizes her father may have been covering for her mother—or being coerced. Beat: the mystery pivots from whether to who.

chapters.title: Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Ivo meets Tomas Brandt, who receives her with unnerving gentleness and refuses to discuss the case: 'The law had its say. I don't get a second one.' He asks instead about her mother's songs. Ivo leaves furious, then understands he is protecting someone too. Beat: compassion complicating justice; the law shown as insufficient.

chapters.title: Vera's Last Tape
chapters.summary: Vera, declining rapidly, gives Ivo a second reel she'd forgotten: a 1981 interview with Ivo's mother, recorded in secret, in which she nearly names the true arsonist—her own brother-in-law, the village's beloved benefactor—before stopping herself. Vera dies three days later. Beat: midpoint climax; the benefactor revealed as suspect.

chapters.title: The Benefactor
chapters.summary: Ivo researches Aurel Danek: philanthropist, church pillar, dead ten years, family still prominent. Evidence aligns—insurance records, the fire's origin point, his sudden emigration. But he is beyond the law's reach, and exposing him means accusing a dynasty with lawyers and a town's gratitude. Beat: justice outside the law becomes the only road.

chapters.title: Translation Under Pressure
chapters.summary: With the digitized audio failing, Ivo makes her final transcription alone at night, Kavreni returning to her in floods as if summoned by purpose. She completes the sentence: her father confessed because Danek threatened to deport the family's undocumented relatives—duty weaponized into silence. Beat: the untranslatable sentence translated; Ivo weeps in a language she thought she'd lost.

chapters.title: What Tomas Asks For
chapters.summary: Ivo returns to Brandt with the full truth. He finally speaks: he always knew, forgave her father long ago, and asks not for exoneration but for the record—one document, filed, so the lie isn't the last word. His health fails sharply. Beat: grace; the definition of justice narrows to witness.

chapters.title: The Document
chapters.summary: Ivo drafts the translation with sworn annotations, facing legal threats from the Danek estate and Marisol's final plea. She signs it with her full name—her first public act as herself rather than as a conduit. Filing it, she feels neither triumph nor ruin but weight leaving. Beat: climax resolved through choice, not victory.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The filing leaks; a journalist pieces together the story. The Danek family denies everything; historians take notice; Brandt's conviction is formally reviewed posthumously—he dies the week the review opens, having heard the news. Ivo attends no cameras. Beat: bittersweet vindication; justice done quietly, imperfectly, truly.

chapters.title: The Song, Sung Back
chapters.summary: At Brandt's small funeral, Ivo sings her mother's song in restored Kavreni before strangers who don't understand the words—and doesn't need them to. Marisol takes her hand. Some words have gone dark forever; Ivo lets them go. Beat: reconciliation with loss itself; language as inheritance, not possession.

chapters.title: Ulyana and the Interior
chapters.summary: Epilogue, one year later: Ivo teaches community translation classes and keeps a notebook of returning Kavreni words, titled with her mother's name, Ulyana. On the radio, the song plays again—now credited. She smiles at a stranger, and this time the smile begins a conversation. Final beat: the interior made exterior; invisibility voluntarily ended.
